title: People v. Landis et al. (Twilight Zone manslaughter trial)
who: John Landis; George Folsey Jr.; Dan Allingham; Dorcey Wingo; Paul Stewart; Deputy DA Lea Purwin D'Agostino
description: Director John Landis, associate producer George Folsey Jr., production manager Dan Allingham, helicopter pilot Dorcey Wingo and explosives specialist Paul Stewart were charged with involuntary manslaughter over the deaths of Vic Morrow, Myca Dinh Le and Renee Shin-Yi Chen. After a ten-month trial in Los Angeles in 1986-87, prosecuted by Lea Purwin D'Agostino, a jury acquitted all five in May 1987. The defense argued that the explosion that brought down the helicopter could not have been foreseen.

The Christian Science Monitor reported on the new set-safety guidelines while the trial was under way.
why: These reforms are a lasting legacy of the franchise's darkest event.

title: The six videotaped episodes of season 2
who: CBS; Rod Serling; Buck Houghton
description: To cut costs in the second season, six episodes were recorded on videotape on a studio stage with four cameras, cut together like a live broadcast: 'The Lateness of the Hour', 'The Night of the Meek', 'The Whole Truth', 'Twenty Two', 'Static' and 'Long Distance Call'. They saved only about $6,000 each and made location work almost impossible, so the experiment was not repeated. Serling called the result neither fish nor fowl, and kinescope copies were later used in syndication.

title: Marius Constant's fight for rights to the Twilight Zone theme
who: Marius Constant; CBS
description: Constant was paid about $200 to deliver a theme overnight, plus $500 if it was used, and his check took three months to arrive. He later sued and won rights to future earnings from the music, although not from past uses. The Seattle Times told the story in 1997.
why: It explains who owns and profits from the franchise's best-known piece of music.

sources.title: Seattle Times (1997) - In Composer's Past: 'Twilight Zone' Theme
MeTV - The Twilight Zone theme song composer called himself the most popular unknown composer in America

title: Nike's offer to license the Twilight Zone theme
who: Marius Constant; Nike
description: According to the Seattle Times, Nike offered Constant $3,000 to use his theme in a commercial. He asked for $100,000 and agreed to $80,000, but the music never ran in a Nike ad. The story shows how much advertisers valued the theme as an instant signal of strangeness.
why: It shows the commercial value of the theme decades after the show ended.

sources.title: Seattle Times (1997) - In Composer's Past: 'Twilight Zone' Theme

title: Merriam-Webster entry: 'twilight zone'
who: Merriam-Webster
description: Merriam-Webster defines 'twilight zone' as an area just beyond the usual limits, such as those of law or ethics, and also as a realm of fantasy or illusion. It dates the first sense to 1908, so the phrase existed before the show. The 'fantasy' sense is the one Serling's series made widespread, and the dictionary's example sentences show both in use.
why: It documents how the show's title became an everyday English expression.

title: 'Submitted for your approval'
who: Rod Serling
description: Although it is the phrase most associated with Serling, he says it word for word in only three episodes: 'Cavender Is Coming', 'In Praise of Pip' and 'A Kind of a Stopwatch'. Close variants such as 'for your consideration' appear elsewhere, and he says 'in just a moment' far more often. The phrase is now a standard opener for parodies and for anyone imitating Serling.
why: It is the show's best-known catchphrase.

sources.title: SYFY - The Twilight Zone's most iconic catchphrase was barely ever said
Cheat Sheet - Serling's signature phrase was only uttered in 3 episodes

title: 'It's a cookbook!'
who: Damon Knight (story); Rod Serling (teleplay); Lloyd Bochner
description: The twist line of 'To Serve Man', adapted from Damon Knight's short story, has become shorthand for an offer that seems kind but hides a trap. The Simpsons parodied it in a Treehouse of Horror segment, where Lisa's discovery of the aliens' book 'How to Cook Humans' turns out to be a misreading, and the line is endlessly quoted and spoofed.
why: It is the series' most quoted twist line.

title: The Simpsons' 'Treehouse of Horror' and Twilight Zone parodies
who: The Simpsons writers; Fox
description: From its first Halloween special in 1990, The Simpsons' 'Treehouse of Horror' episodes have regularly parodied Twilight Zone stories, including 'To Serve Man', 'It's a Good Life', 'Nightmare at 20,000 Feet', 'Living Doll' and 'The Monsters Are Due on Maple Street'. Bart often delivers a Serling-style introduction. SYFY has catalogued every one of these parodies.
tz_refs: The Monsters Are Due on Maple Street
why: These are some of the most-watched tributes that keep the show's stories familiar to new viewers.

title: The theme's guitar motif as a shorthand for 'weird'
who: Marius Constant; CBS
description: The repeating guitar figure from Constant's theme, usually hummed as 'doo-doo-doo-doo', has become a common way to say that something is uncanny. It is played at pro basketball games, was recorded by the Manhattan Transfer, and was listed by TIME in 2010 among television's ten most unforgettable sounds.
why: It is the franchise's most widespread borrowing in everyday culture.

title: 'Something on the wing' and the airline 'Shatner seat'
who: Richard Matheson; William Shatner
description: 'Nightmare at 20,000 Feet', in which William Shatner's character sees a gremlin on the wing, has made the gremlin a standard joke about nervous flyers. MeTV and BGR report that some crews and frequent flyers call the window seat under the small black triangles above the wing the 'Shatner seat', although no airline has confirmed where the nickname came from.
why: It shows an episode becoming part of how people talk about air travel.

title: 'The Monsters Are Due on Maple Street' as a commentary touchstone
who: Rod Serling; columnists and educators
description: Serling's story of neighbors turning on each other during a blackout is often cited by columnists writing about mass suspicion, scapegoating and moral panic, from the McCarthy era to the 2020 pandemic. It is also widely taught in schools. TIME named it one of the ten best episodes in 2009, and the 2002 revival remade it as a story about fear of terrorism.

The Monsters Are on Maple Street (2003)
why: It is the episode most often used as political shorthand.

title: The broken glasses of 'Time Enough at Last'
who: Burgess Meredith; Rod Serling; Lynn Venable (story)
description: Burgess Meredith's bookworm, alone after a nuclear war with all the time in the world to read, breaks his glasses. The image has become shorthand for cruel irony and has been parodied and referenced many times. The episode, based on a story by Lynn Venable, regularly tops lists of the best episodes.
why: It is one of the most recognizable images from the series.

description: Robby, the Forbidden Planet robot that MGM later loaned to The Twilight Zone, sold at Bonhams New York for $5,375,000, then a record for a film prop at auction. On the show, Robby appeared in 'Uncle Simon' and in 'The Brain Center at Whipple's'.

who: MGM; Cayuga Productions
description: The Twilight Zone borrowed MGM's miniatures and full-size set pieces of the Forbidden Planet starship. title: Original 'Eye of the Beholder' pig-face mask at auction
who: William Tuttle (makeup designer); auction consignor
description: In late 2018 an original prosthetic mask from 'Eye of the Beholder', one of William Tuttle's pig-like faces for the hospital staff, went up for auction. It drew coverage from Gizmodo, CBC Radio's As It Happens and HuffPost. Masks from the episode rarely survive and are among the most sought-after Twilight Zone props.
why: It is one of the show's most famous makeup effects and is known to survive.

description: Heritage Auctions offered Matheson's own typed and hand-annotated script, with related materials, for his third-season comedy 'Once Upon a Time', which starred Buster Keaton. Writers' working scripts like this are a major part of the market for Twilight Zone paper collectibles.

title: The original Talky Tina doll
who: June Foray (voice); Vogue Dolls (Brikette, reported base doll)
description: Talky Tina in 'Living Doll' is widely reported to have been a modified version of Vogue's 'Brikette' doll, with June Foray, voice of the Chatty Cathy toy, providing its voice. Doll collectors' blogs track surviving Brikettes for this reason, but the fate of the screen-used doll is not publicly documented.
why: Tina is one of the most iconic objects in the show.
